summary:
Buenos Aires province stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passage by the Chamber of Deputies by 167 votes to 17 and by the Senate by 55 votes to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains in force in the province.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. A national decree of December 2024 added consent and medical-judicial requirements for minors' gender-affirming care and is under litigation. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors, reported by Reuters as banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents, together with a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

The province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in the country on police conduct. The provincial ombudsman's Gender Violence Office, created by Resolución Nº 100/10, submitted a report to the UN Human Rights Committee for its review of June and July 2016 documenting violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police, or by third parties acting under police cover, against trans and travesti people, in a dedicated section on violence by judicial, state and police agents. The documented incidents occurred in three cities: La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría, carried out under preventive policing frameworks.

Academic legal analysis identifies a second, indirect instrument of criminalisation. In 2005 Buenos Aires province assumed jurisdiction over drug-sale and possession offences, a devolution that enabled provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution to become the operative mechanism of indirect criminalisation of travesti and trans women after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence. A UNLP thesis documents the pattern through microtrafficking enforcement in La Plata's Zona Roja, and Pensamiento Penal records rising criminalisation of trans and travesti women in the province, particularly in that district.

For a trans visitor the operative exposure is police contact: any stop, identity check or street offence in the province engages a documented history of state-implicated violence and of drug and street-offence charges used as a proxy for trans presence. Detention therefore carries a specific, sourced risk rather than a generic one.

Placement in custody is governed by a national rule. In February 2025 the Milei government banned housing trans women convicted of sexual crimes, human trafficking, or any violent crime against a woman in a women's prison. The rule restricts women's-prison housing for trans women in those conviction categories, and no separate trans housing unit or other trans-specific placement rule is recorded; Buenos Aires province has no trans-specific placement rule of its own.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a figure described as a record and as averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes called it an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the country, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravation is not currently applied in that line of cases.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, nonetheless records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.

The provincial pattern sits inside a national deterioration rather than standing apart from it: the December 2024 decree on minors' care and the February 2025 decrees apply countrywide, while the police-conduct findings and the drug-law proxy prosecution are provincial in origin.
localsOnly:
The provincial Ombudsman published a guide in September 2024 to gender-marker rectification for people born in Buenos Aires province, setting out registry rectification steps under the recognition regime established by the 2012 federal Gender Identity Law. The guide includes provisions for people born in the province who now live elsewhere, so rectification can be completed without returning to the birth jurisdiction.

Residents who are minors face the consent and medical-judicial requirements introduced by the December 2024 decree for gender-affirming care, a measure whose legality is being contested in court, alongside the February 2025 decree restricting surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Adult legal gender recognition under Law 26.743 is unaffected by those measures on the face of the sources.

Provincial residents held in custody are subject to the national February 2025 housing rule rather than to any provincial policy, since Buenos Aires province has recorded no trans-specific placement rule and no separate trans housing unit.

Provincial street-offence and drug-law prosecution, following the 2005 devolution of drug-sale and possession jurisdiction to provincial justice, is the mechanism through which trans and travesti women in the province have been drawn into the criminal process, with La Plata's Zona Roja the documented focus.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the litigation against the December 2024 decree on minors' gender-affirming care has produced a ruling, and whether the February 2025 decrees have been challenged or modified in court. The sources record the legal challenge as intended and the decree as in force, with no outcome stated.

Unresolved: whether the police conduct documented in the 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee persists in the same form. The inventory supplies no post-2016 provincial evidence of police violence against trans and travesti people, and no enforcement data on the drug and street-offence prosecutions after the 2005 devolution.

Unresolved: whether the travesticidio aggravating circumstance has been applied in any Buenos Aires province case since the April 2025 Supreme Court decision left the removal of the aggravation in the Sacayán case standing. No provincial homicide data is sourced.

Not sourced: hate-crime counts broken down to the province, the number of gender-marker rectifications completed under the September 2024 guide, and any provincial rule on placement of trans detainees awaiting trial as distinct from sentenced prisoners.
